newsitem.title: FRANCE: France alarmed by counterfeiters on the Internet.
newsitem.headline: France alarmed by counterfeiters on the Internet.

text.p: The Internet is turning out to be a fabulous tool for counterfeiters, who are tapping into the open network to relay pictures of French fashions across the globe to sweatshops turning out fakes, French officials said on Thursday.

"Less than 24 hours after the fashion shows, photos from all the collections are made public around the world through the Internet," the French anti-counterfeiting task force CNAC said in its annual report.
It said authorities had opened two investigations of counterfeiting operations using the Internet, an unregulated, worldwide network connecting computer systems.
But the head of the CNAC, formed last year as part of a strict 1994 anti-counterfeiting law, said the agency had not worked out a strategy to stop counterfeiters from using the Net.
"We haven't yet organised ourselves," Ladislas Poniatowski told a news conference. "Our work is similar to that of (medical) researchers -- the more we advance, the more the viruses adapt or mutate."
High tech counterfeiters are also targeting the video and software industries, but France's world-renowned fashion and perfume houses remain the prime targets, he said.
The Industry Ministry estimates the huge business in counterfeit goods costs the French economy between 25 billion and 30 billion francs ($5.8 billion) a year and represents 30,000 jobs.
France is particularly vulnerable, with seven out of 10 fakes copying a French product, according to the ministry.

The bulk of counterfeit goods seized by French customs are made in Taiwan, Thailand and Turkey. But the CNAC report said counterfeit production is on the rise in Vietnam, Indonesia, Pakistan, India, the United States and some parts of Africa.

France stiffened penalties for counterfeiters in 1994 to include prison sentences of up to two years and fines of up to one million francs, and it stepped up efforts to crack down on the production of fakes.

The number of seizures by customs officials rose 45 percent in 1995 to nearly 300,000 articles from 1994, the number of Paris tribunal convictions rose to 40 from 26, and prosecutions and detentions are both up nearly 50 percent, Poniatowski said.
The CNAC's objectives are to increase financial assistance to small French companies lacking the resources trease international cooperation to convince other governments to take a tougher approach.

France sent missions last year to Saudi Arabia, Russia and China last year and signed a cooperation accord with China. But Poniatowski said many Asian countries, such as Vietnam, Indonesia and South Korea, allow counterfeiting operations or, as in South Korea's case, the manufacture of "similar brands".

Even France's neighbours, Belgium and Luxembourg, have not passed legislation to deter counterfeiters, and France views as over-generous the European Union regulations restricting the value of counterfeit goods that travellers may bring into Europe. ($ = 5.14 French Francs)
